title: Screen Restriction Is Not Pedagogical Reform
author: Potkalitsky, Nick
summary: A careful reading of the empirical research on school phone bans reveals that restriction produces real but narrowly targeted benefits: test score gains are concentrated among struggling students and in schools where pre-ban phone use was highest, with the most disadvantaged students gaining the most. Mental health findings are contested and unevenly gendered, with Norwegian data showing reduced specialist visits for girls but no benefit for boys. Bullying reductions are more consistent across studies. The critical variable is not the policy itself but implementation fidelity -- schools that prohibited phones but left devices in bags saw minimal effects, while hard all-day enforcement produced measurable gains. The deeper problem with screen time cap legislation is what it cannot do: produce a lasting change in how students relate to their devices. None of the phone ban studies demonstrates that restriction teaches digital wellness or self-regulatory capacity; when students leave the building, the same patterns of use resume. The author argues that educators who want a seat at the policy table need to arrive with something more specific than defensiveness and more ambitious than a ban.
points: * The most robust finding across multiple studies is that phone bans help struggling students disproportionately: the lowest-achieving quartile gains significantly while the highest quartile gains essentially nothing. * Implementation dose determines everything: restriction that leaves phones in bags produces minimal effects; hard, consistently enforced, all-day policies produce measurable downstream gains. * The Florida research found a first-year enforcement spike in suspensions concentrated among Black students -- a serious equity signal that implementation plans must explicitly address. * Phone bans produce behavioral and academic gains during school hours; they produce no evidence that students develop different relationships to their devices afterward. * The infrastructure required to teach digital wellness -- high-quality offline materials, IEP-aware protocols, department-level budget management -- does not yet exist in most districts.
quotes: The studies that find measurable effects are almost uniformly the ones that describe hard, consistently enforced, all-day policies where the intervention dose was real.

None of the phone ban studies produced evidence that restriction teaches anything about digital wellness and literacy. The ban ends at dismissal. The student walks out of school with the same patterns of use.
Restriction is a starting point, not a solution, and the educators who understand the difference are the ones who need to be in the room when the implementation guidance gets written.
A screen time cap written into state law and then implemented inconsistently across six periods, three grade levels, and two union contracts is not the same intervention the research studied.
